messages.subject: Feedback on oSCR cheat sheet
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone! I was wondering if I could ask you a favor. I designed a cheet sheet for oSCR (see attachment) and before I release it into the wild aka Twitter and RStudio Cheet Sheet Repository, I was wondering if you could take a look and provide feedback or comments on it. After all, you have used oSCR and are familiar with the program. Andy, Chris, and Dan have seen it and said it was ok to post it here.

I'm asking for feedback on everything (colors, organization, etc.) but mostly on how well I explained the functions, and if they are clear enough, or if there is something I should have included that I didn't, or should remove because it's too confusing. Leave your comments here on this post so we can all see them.

Thank you in advance!

messages.subject: which encounter model for live trapping data?
messages.subject_clean: which encounter model for live trapping data?
messages.body_plain:
Hello Everyone,
I have a live-trapping dataset for voles, and I'm wondering which encounter model to use.

The issue is that once a trap is occupied, it's not available for others to occupy. I have a note from Chris from the SMBI workshop this summer that I should use encmod=M. However when I read the documentation it sounds like this is used mainly when you have the chance of capturing more than 1 individual in each trap, which isn't my situation.

Chris and others, what would you recommend?

I should add that I'm not sure how necessary it is to correct for this, based on what I'm reading in the literature. Our trap checks were every 8 hours, traps were pretty close together (every 10m), and trap saturation was low enough (on average 4.5 traps occupied per 100 traps available each check) that we might not need to worry about this. Does anyone else have experience or thoughts on this issue?

Thanks for the help! Karen

Based on the situation you describe (check frequency and saturation), the 'multicatch' model should be absolutely fine.

You can convince yourself of this but reading this nice paper by Greg Distiller and David Botchers:

A spatially explicit capture–recapture estimator for single‐catch traps

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/ece3.1748

messages.subject: RE: extract.raster() Clarification Question
messages.body_plain:
Hi David (responded also to oSCR list),

I think I posted a response to a similar question, which reminded me I need to integrate this updated version of the function to the package. For the time being, run this code:

extract.rast2 <- function(ss, rast, mult = 1, cov.name <http://cov.name> = "val.1",
                          buffer=NULL, method="simple", fun = mean){
  for(i in 1:length(ss)){
    tmpS <- ss[[i]][, c("X", "Y")] * mult
    r1 <- raster::extract(rast, tmpS, buffer=buffer, fun = fun, na.rm=T)
    ss[[i]][, cov.name <http://cov.name>] <- r1
  }
  return(ss)
}

if your raster is a single layer, the cov.name <http://cov.name> should be a single character you want to name the covariate in the ssDF. If it’s a stack/brick, then provide a vector of names and multiple columns will be generated. The mult argument is useful when you divide UTM coordinates by something to change from, e.g., m to km, in which case you’d do mult=1000. The buffer argument defined the buffer around the point to summarize the values, and the fun argument defines how to summarize.

Note, though, that this function assumes the single raster or raster stack encompasses ALL state space points.

(I guess I just wrote the help file J)

Chris
